conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for making time today. I’m <med>Dr. Ramirez</med>, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you settle into life with your new baby.

We’re going to use a short questionnaire called the <sym>Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)</sym>. It’s a 10-question screen that looks at how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days. It’s not a test, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. Everything you share stays confidential, and we’ll go at your pace so you feel safe and comfortable.

When you’re ready, I’ll ask each question conversationally. If you need me to repeat anything or you’re unsure how to answer, just let me know. Ready to start?

Over the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not much. I used to laugh all the time—my husband and I would joke about everything—but lately it feels like I’m just… flat. I’ll smile if someone shows me a cute video or if the baby does something funny, but it’s not the same. It’s like I’m watching life through a fog. Maybe once or twice this week I caught myself actually laughing, but it faded fast.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… I mean, I *have* laughed a little, but it’s not the same. It feels forced or like I’m just going through the motions. Most of the time I’m too tired or worried to really feel it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like one more thing I have to get through. I’ll think “maybe tomorrow I’ll feel like myself again,” but when tomorrow comes it’s the same heavy feeling.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

All the time. If the baby won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I’m not holding him right, or my milk isn’t good enough, or I missed his sleepy cues. Yesterday he cried for almost an hour and I kept replaying every little thing I’d done, convinced it was my fault. My head knows babies just cry, but I still feel like I’m failing him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart starts racing because I’m sure he’s not breathing right, or I’ll lie awake counting his breaths through the monitor. There’s no real reason—his check-ups are fine—but I can’t shake the dread that something awful is about to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… it’s like a sudden wave of fear out of nowhere. A couple nights ago I was just rocking the baby in the dark and my chest got tight, heart pounding, like I had to run out of the room. No warning, no reason—I knew I was safe, but my body felt like we were in danger. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky and crying.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like the second I finish one feeding, the next is due, or the laundry’s piled up again, or I’ve forgotten to eat. I keep thinking, “How does anyone do this?” I manage—he’s always fed, changed, loved—but it’s like I’m barely treading water. Some afternoons I just sit on the couch while he naps and stare at the wall because I can’t figure out what to tackle first.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I’ll finally get him down, but then my mind starts spinning—did I burp him long enough, is he still breathing, what if he wakes up the second I fall asleep? Some nights I lie there for hours, exhausted but wide-awake, listening to every tiny sound. Even when I do drift off, I jerk awake sure I heard him cry. I probably get three broken hours, if I’m lucky.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like there’s a gray cloud parked over me. I’ll be changing his diaper and tears just start leaking out. I keep thinking I should feel grateful—he’s healthy, I wanted him so badly—but the sadness is just… there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried three, maybe four times since last weekend. Yesterday it was because I spilled the pumped milk I’d spent twenty minutes getting. I sat on the kitchen floor sobbing like the world had ended while the baby slept in the next room. It’s never about just the milk—it’s everything piling up and that was the final straw.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I feel low, but I’d never want to leave my baby or my husband like that. I just want the sadness and the fear to lift so I can enjoy being a mom.

Your words paint a tender, painful picture of early motherhood right now: the laughter that used to come easily now feels forced, the tasks that once brought joy feel like obstacles, and a gray cloud of sadness settles over most days. You're pouring every ounce of energy into caring for your baby while intrusive worries about his safety race through your mind and keep you awake at night. Even when you finally lie down, your body jerks awake, certain you've heard him cry. Sitting on the kitchen floor sobbing over spilled milk, you described feeling like the world had ended-an image that captures how overwhelmed and depleted you feel. Yet amid the tears, you remain steadfastly devoted to your son and determined to find your way back to the confident, light-hearted person you know yourself to be.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to enjoy humor, describing laughter as forced and infrequent, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself 'All the time' and gives multiple detailed examples, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily, intrusive, medically-unfounded worries about the baby's breathing that disrupt sleep and feeding, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart, urge to flee) without any identifiable trigger, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily overwhelm and difficulty coping, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly, prolonged insomnia driven by persistent anxiety and low mood, aligning with 'most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive daily sadness with spontaneous tearfulness, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes in a week triggered by stress, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS score of 24 far exceeds the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major depression. You endorse core symptoms daily: diminished interest or pleasure (Q2 score 3), depressed mood most of the day (Q8 score 3), feelings of worthlessness/guilt (Q3 score 3), sleep disruption driven by low mood (Q7 score 3), recurrent crying (Q9 score 2), and concentration difficulties from feeling overwhelmed (Q6 score 2). <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> require ≥5 symptoms during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum; you meet mood, interest, guilt, sleep, and concentration criteria plus anxiety/panic symptoms that often coexist. Although you denied self-harm thoughts (Q10 score 0), functional impairment is considerable and warrants urgent evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary-care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and discuss risks/benefits of <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Reach out today to supportive family or friends who can help with household tasks, night feeds, or simply sit with you so you can nap
4. Practice brief self-care: five-minute showers, stepping outside for daylight, and eating small frequent snacks to stabilize mood and energy
5. Limit stimulants and screen time before bed; consider rotating night duties with a partner to allow 3-4 hour uninterrupted sleep blocks
6. Keep the baby-safe helpline numbers handy: <med>Postpartum Support International</med> 1-800-944-4773 or local emergency services if distress escalates
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screen  
Date: [Today’s date]  Source: Patient self-report (EPDS-style items)

A. Positive indicators  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness most days  
- Marked anhedonia (minimal enjoyment, activities feel burdensome)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt re infant care  
- Daily, non-specific anxiety + episodic panic (physical surge, no clear trigger)  
- Sleep disturbance driven by intrusive worry about infant safety  
- Sense of being overwhelmed, “treading water,” difficulty prioritizing tasks  

B. Frequency/severity  
- Crying spells ≥3×/week; sleep ≤3 hrs fragmented nightly  
- Panic episode(s) with autonomic symptoms; anticipatory worry between feeds  

C. Safety  
- Denies self-harm or suicidal ideation (endorsed item 10 “never”)  
- No current intent or plan noted  

D. Screening significance  
Pattern consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depressive symptoms with comorbid anxiety; functional impact evident in self-care and caregiving confidence.  

E. Recommendations for clinician  
1. Complete standardized EPDS scoring; document total.  
2. Assess for obsessive/intrusive thoughts about infant safety.  
3. Consider differential: postpartum anxiety disorder, OCD, or depressive episode with anxious distress.  
4. Provide psycho-education, support resources; discuss treatment options (evidence-based therapy and/or medication).  
5. Schedule follow-up within 1 week; monitor safety at every contact.
